lessons.title: Blast Furnace Design and Operation
lessons.body: A blast furnace is a tall, vertical shaft furnace used to smelt iron ore into molten iron. In Africa, small-scale blast furnaces are often built from local clay or steel drums lined with firebrick. The furnace is charged from the top with alternating layers of iron ore, coke (or charcoal), and limestone. A hot air blast (often preheated to 600â1000Â°C) is blown into the bottom through tuyeres. The coke burns, producing carbon monoxide that reduces the iron ore to iron. The molten iron and slag collect at the bottom and are tapped periodically. Key design parameters include the furnace height (typically 5â30 meters for industrial units, but 1â3 meters for small-scale), the diameter of the hearth, and the number of tuyeres. In Africa, charcoal is often used instead of coke because of its availability, but it is weaker and can crush under the burden, so the furnace must be shorter. Operation requires careful control of the charge ratio: for every 1 kg of iron ore, you need about 0.5â1 kg of coke and 0.2â0.5 kg of limestone. The blast volume should be around 100â200 mÂ³ per minute per square meter of hearth area. Temperature zones: preheating (200â800Â°C), reduction (800â1100Â°C), and melting (1200â1600Â°C). Tapping is done every 2â4 hours. Safety: always wear leather aprons, face shields, and gloves. Never stand in front of the tap hole. In Nigeria, the Ajaokuta Steel Plant uses large blast furnaces, but small foundries in Kenya and Tanzania use cupola-like furnaces for cast iron. Regular maintenance includes checking for cracks in the refractory lining and replacing tuyeres when they burn out.

lessons.title: Electric Arc Furnace Fundamentals
lessons.body: An electric arc furnace (EAF) uses high-voltage electric arcs to melt scrap metal or directly reduced iron. It is common in South Africa, Egypt, and Nigeria for steel production. The furnace is a large cylindrical vessel with a removable roof through which three graphite electrodes descend. When the electrodes touch the scrap, an arc forms, generating temperatures up to 3000Â°C. The furnace is lined with refractory bricks, usually magnesite or dolomite, because the slag is basic. A typical EAF for a small African foundry might have a capacity of 1â5 tonnes. Power supply is critical: a 1-tonne furnace needs about 500â800 kVA. The transformer steps down high voltage to low voltage (200â600 V) but high current (10,000â50,000 A). Charging is done by opening the roof and dropping scrap in a bucket. Melting takes 30â60 minutes. After melting, you add alloying elements and tap the steel into a ladle. Slag is removed by tilting the furnace. In Africa, EAFs are often used because they can melt locally available scrap, reducing dependence on imported coke. However, electricity supply can be unreliable, so many operators use diesel generators as backup. Key operating parameters: arc length (controlled by electrode position), power input (adjusted by transformer taps), and foamy slag practice (injecting carbon and oxygen to create a foamy slag that shields the arcs and reduces heat loss). Safety: never touch electrodes or water-cooled cables. Wear arc-rated clothing. In South Africa, companies like Scaw Metals use large EAFs, while small workshops in Ghana use 1-tonne units.

lessons.title: Reverberatory Furnace Principles
lessons.body: A reverberatory furnace is a rectangular or cylindrical furnace where the charge is melted by heat reflected from the roof and walls. It is used for melting copper, tin, and aluminum, and for refining metals. In Africa, it is common in small-scale copper smelting in Zambia and the DRC. The furnace has a shallow hearth, a curved roof, and a chimney at one end. Fuel (coal, oil, or gas) is burned in a firebox at one end, and the hot gases pass over the charge and exit through the chimney. The roof is made of high-alumina bricks to withstand temperatures up to 1600Â°C. The hearth is lined with magnesite or chrome-magnesite bricks. The charge is introduced through doors on the side. Melting occurs primarily by radiation from the roof, so the roof must be kept hot. A typical small reverberatory furnace might be 2 m long, 1 m wide, and 1 m high, with a capacity of 500 kg. Fuel consumption is high: about 1â2 kg of coal per kg of metal melted. To improve efficiency, preheat the combustion air using a recuperator. The slag is tapped from a notch at the side, and metal is tapped from a lower notch. In Zambia, the Nkana smelter uses large reverberatory furnaces for copper. For a learner, key points: keep the roof clean, maintain a slightly oxidizing atmosphere to burn off sulfur, and avoid overcharging. Safety: wear heat-resistant gloves and face shields. Never open the charging door while the burner is on full blast.

lessons.title: Flash Smelting Furnace Technology
lessons.body: Flash smelting is a pyrometallurgical process for smelting sulfide ores, especially copper and nickel. It was developed in Finland but is used in Africa at large mines like Kansanshi in Zambia and Tenke Fungurume in the DRC. In flash smelting, dry concentrate is injected with oxygen-enriched air or pure oxygen into a hot furnace. The particles ignite and burn instantly, generating their own heat. The furnace is a tall, vertical shaft with a reaction chamber at the top and a settler at the bottom. The reaction shaft is lined with chrome-magnesite bricks, and the settler is lined with magnesite-chrome bricks. Temperatures reach 1300â1400Â°C. The products are a matte (molten metal sulfide) and a slag. The matte is tapped and further processed, while the slag is discarded or reprocessed. Key design parameters: oxygen enrichment (typically 30â70% oxygen), concentrate feed rate (e.g., 50â100 tonnes per hour for large units), and furnace pressure (slightly negative to prevent gas leakage). For small-scale operations, flash smelting is not practical because it requires fine, dry concentrate and sophisticated gas handling. However, the principles are useful to understand. In Africa, flash smelting is used at the Kansanshi smelter in Zambia, which produces about 300,000 tonnes of copper per year. Safety: the main hazards are sulfur dioxide gas and molten material. Always wear self-contained breathing apparatus when working near the reaction shaft. The off-gas is rich in SO2 and is captured to make sulfuric acid.

lessons.title: Crucible and Cupola Furnaces
lessons.body: Crucible furnaces are simple: a clay-graphite or silicon carbide crucible is placed inside a furnace heated by coke, oil, or gas. The metal is melted in the crucible, not in contact with the fuel, so it is clean. They are ideal for melting small amounts (5â50 kg) of aluminum, brass, bronze, and precious metals. In Africa, crucible furnaces are common in artisanal gold and jewelry workshops in Ghana, Mali, and South Africa. A typical furnace is a steel drum lined with firebrick, with a hole for the crucible and a lid. Fuel is coke or LPG. Melting times: 30â60 minutes for aluminum, 1â2 hours for copper alloys. Temperature control is by adjusting air supply. Crucibles must be preheated to avoid cracking. Cupola furnaces are vertical shaft furnaces used for melting cast iron. They are like small blast furnaces but simpler. The cupola is charged with alternate layers of coke, limestone, and scrap iron. Air is blown through tuyeres near the bottom. The coke burns, melting the iron, which trickles down and is tapped continuously. A typical cupola is 1â3 m tall and 0.5â1 m in diameter, melting 1â5 tonnes per hour. In Africa, cupolas are used in foundries in Nigeria, Kenya, and Zimbabwe. Key operating parameters: coke-to-iron ratio (1:8 to 1:12), blast rate (80â150 mÂ³/min per mÂ²), and tuyere size. Safety: cupolas produce carbon monoxide, so good ventilation is essential. Never tap molten iron into a wet ladleâit will explode.

lessons.title: Refractory Materials and Furnace Linings
lessons.body: Refractory materials are heat-resistant materials used to line furnaces. They must withstand high temperatures, thermal shock, chemical attack from slag and gases, and mechanical wear. In Africa, common refractories include fireclay bricks (for temperatures up to 1200Â°C), high-alumina bricks (up to 1600Â°C), magnesite bricks (basic, for steel furnaces), and chrome-magnesite bricks (for copper and nickel furnaces). For small-scale furnaces, locally made clay bricks mixed with sawdust or rice husks can be used, but they have lower performance. The lining is installed in layers: an insulating layer (e.g., diatomaceous earth) against the steel shell, then a firebrick layer, then a working lining of high-alumina or magnesite bricks. The working lining is the sacrificial layer that contacts the melt. Mortar must match the brick type: fireclay mortar for firebricks, magnesite mortar for magnesite bricks. Expansion joints are needed to allow for thermal expansion. In Africa, refractory suppliers include Vesuvius in South Africa and local brick makers in Nigeria. Maintenance: inspect linings after every campaign. Cracks can be patched with refractory cement. A lining typically lasts 6â24 months depending on operation. For a small foundry, a 1-tonne cupola might need 200â300 firebricks. Safety: always wear a dust mask when cutting or grinding refractories; some contain crystalline silica. When installing, ensure bricks are dry and free of moisture to prevent steam explosions during first heat-up.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Furnace Types, Selection & Operating Parameters for African Smelting Operations

This practical reference consolidates the operating envelopes, design parameters, and selection logic for the six furnace families covered in this module. It is written for plant managers, metallurgical engineers, and project developers across Africa's growing non-ferrous and ferrous smelting sector â from copperbelt operations in Zambia and the DRC to ferroalloy plants in South Africa and Zimbabwe, tin and tungsten smelters in Rwanda and Nigeria, and emerging battery-metals processing in Morocco and Tanzania.

The guiding principle is simple: furnace selection is a business decision first and a metallurgical decision second. Capital intensity, energy availability, feed chemistry, scale, and logistics determine viability more often than theoretical thermal efficiency. The tables and checklist below are designed for rapid feasibility screening and day-to-day operating reference.

Table 1: Comparative Operating Envelope of Major Furnace Types

Furnace Type Typical Capacity Energy Source Feed Suitability Capital Intensity Africa Relevance
Blast Furnace 500â15,000 t/d (Fe); 300â1,500 t/d (Pb/Cu matte) Coke, injected coal, hot blast Lumpy ore, sinter, pellets; requires coke strength Very High (US$150â500 M+) South Africa (ArcelorMittal), Zimbabwe (ZISCO legacy)
Electric Arc Furnace 5â150 t/h; ferroalloy SAF 5â60 MVA Electrical (grid or captive hydro) Scrap, DRI, calcined ore, fluxes MediumâHigh (US$20â120 M) South Africa ferrochrome/ferromanganese, Zambia steel, Egypt
Reverberatory Furnace 100â1,000 t/d concentrate Coal, heavy fuel oil, gas Oxide/sulphide fines, secondary materials Medium (US$15â60 M) Zambia (legacy Nkana/ Mufulira), DRC copper
Flash Smelting Furnace 1,000â3,000 t/d concentrate Concentrate combustion + oxygen Dry sulphide concentrate, high S Very High (US$400 Mâ1 B+) Zambia (Kansanshi), DRC (Kamoa-Kakula smelter)
Crucible Furnace 0.1â5 t/d Gas, oil, resistance, induction Clean scrap, precious metals, alloys Low (US$10 kâ500 k) Artisanal/small-scale gold, jewellery, Rwanda tin
Cupola Furnace 1â30 t/h Coke Cast iron scrap, pig iron LowâMedium (US$0.5â5 M) Foundries in South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya

Sources: SAIMM Southern African Pyrometallurgy (multiple editions); Metso Outotec Flash Smelting technical data; Outokumpu historical furnace data; World Bank Mining Investment and Smelting in Sub-Saharan Africa (2021).

Table 2: Key Design Parameters and Typical Ranges

Parameter Blast Furnace EAF / SAF Reverb Flash Crucible / Cupola
Operating temperature (Â°C) 1,400â1,550 hearth; 200â1,000 stack 1,550â1,750 bath 1,200â1,400 bath 1,250â1,400 reaction shaft 1,200â1,500
Energy intensity 12â18 GJ/t HM 400â600 kWh/t (steel); 3,000â4,500 kWh/t (FeCr) 8â14 GJ/t feed Autogenous (S oxidation) 5â15 GJ/t (fuel)
Off-gas SOâ Lowâmedium (sinter dependent) Low (scrap dependent) 2â6% (needs capture) 10â30% (acid plant feed) Negligibleâlow
Refractory hot face Carbon brick, SiC, alumina MgOâC, dolomite, chromeâmag Chromeâmag, silica (roof) Chromeâmag, castable Clay, SiC, graphite
Campaign life 8â20 years 1,500â4,000 heats (lining) 2â8 years 4â10 years Weeksâ2 years
Scale economy threshold >1 Mt/y steel >50 kt/y alloy >100 kt/y Cu conc. >300 kt/y Cu conc. Any niche scale

Sources: SAIMM Pyrometallurgy in Southern Africa; U.S. DOE Energy and Environmental Profile of the U.S. Iron and Steel Industry (2000); Metso Outotec flash furnace operating data; Outokumpu flash smelting design manuals; Engineering Council of South Africa refractory practice notes.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Molten Metal, Off-Gas & Refractory Failure

Molten metal and matte contact with water causes violent steam explosions. In African smelters with seasonal humidity and monsoon/rainy-season water ingress, all furnace floors, launders, and tapholes must be dry, inspected, and covered before tapping. Sulphur dioxide from sulphide smelting is lethal at 100 ppm and immediately dangerous above 500 ppm â flash and reverberatory furnace off-gas systems must have continuous SOâ monitoring, functioning scrubbing or acid plants, and site-wide alarm systems. Refractory lining failure (hot spots, breakthrough) is the leading cause of catastrophic furnace incidents; thermal imaging and regular lining thickness surveys are mandatory, not optional. Never bypass water-cooling, pressure, or gas-detection interlocks. Zambia's OSHA and South Africa's Mine Health and Safety Act (MHSA) both require documented risk assessments for all hot-work and tapping operations. A single molten-metal splash incident can halt production for months â the business case for safety discipline is absolute.

Quick Reference Checklist â Pre-Selection & Operating Readiness

  1. Feed chemistry locked down: assay Cu/Ni/Fe/S, gangue, moisture, and particle size distribution confirmed over at least 6 months of drilling or purchase data before selecting furnace type.
  2. Energy security verified: for EAF/SAF, confirm grid reliability, tariff structure, or captive power (hydro, solar+storage) â African grid instability can destroy EAF economics.
  3. Scale matched to resource: a flash furnace needs >300 kt/y concentrate; a reverb or crucible suits smaller or more variable feed. Do not over-capitalise.
  4. Off-gas and SOâ compliance plan: acid plant, scrubbing, or capture route costed and permitted before construction â regulators in Zambia, DRC, and South Africa increasingly enforce SOâ limits.
  5. Refractory supply chain secured: identify local vs imported brick/ castable sources, lead times, and lining installation skills â a 6-month refractory delay can idle a smelter.
  6. Water and cooling strategy: closed-circuit cooling, dry floor policy, and rainy-season protection for tapholes and launders.
  7. Skilled workforce and training plan: furnace operators, tappers, and refractory crews require certified training â partner with SAIMM, universities, or OEM training centres.
  8. Financial model includes campaign life and relining: budget relining intervals, consumable costs, and metal recovery losses â not just construction capex.

Further Reading â Free Official Sources

  • Southern African Institute of Mining and Metallurgy (SAIMM) â free conference proceedings on pyrometallurgy, furnace design, and African smelting practice.
  • Metso Outotec (now Metso) Technical Library â flash smelting and electric furnace technical brochures and design guidance.
  • U.S. Department of Energy â Energy and Environmental Profile of the U.S. Iron and Steel Industry â free PDF with blast furnace and EAF energy data.
  • World Bank â Extractive Industries / Mining in Africa â reports on smelting investment, infrastructure, and regional value chains.
  • International Copper Association / Copper Alliance â free technical resources on copper smelting and furnace operations.

Prepared for RISE AFRICA Skills â Smelting Fundamentals, Module: Furnace Types and Design. This practical reference is for training and feasibility screening; detailed design must be validated by qualified metallurgical engineers and OEM data for each specific project.

quiz.q: What is the primary fuel used in a small-scale blast furnace in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Charcoal is widely used in Africa because of its availability and low cost.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of limestone in a blast furnace?
options: B) To remove impurities as slag
quiz.explanation: Limestone (calcium carbonate) reacts with impurities to form slag.

quiz.q: In a blast furnace, where is the hot air blown in?
quiz.explanation: Tuyeres are nozzles near the bottom that inject hot air.

quiz.q: What is the typical tapping temperature range for molten iron in a blast furnace?
quiz.explanation: Molten iron is tapped at around 1200â1600Â°C.

quiz.q: Why are small-scale blast furnaces in Africa often shorter than industrial ones?
options: B) Because charcoal is weaker than coke
D) Because of low ore grade
quiz.explanation: Charcoal has lower crushing strength, so the burden must be lighter, requiring a shorter furnace.

quiz.q: What is the function of graphite electrodes in an electric arc furnace?
options: A) To conduct electricity and create an arc
C) To add carbon to the steel
quiz.explanation: Graphite electrodes carry current and form an arc with the scrap.

quiz.q: What is the typical power supply needed for a 1-tonne electric arc furnace?
quiz.explanation: A 1-tonne EAF typically requires 500â800 kVA.

quiz.q: What is foamy slag practice in an EAF?
options: A) Adding water to the slag
B) Injecting carbon and oxygen to create a foamy slag
quiz.explanation: Foamy slag shields the arcs, reducing heat loss and noise.

quiz.q: Why are EAFs popular in some African countries?
options: A) They can melt local scrap
D) They are simple to build
quiz.explanation: EAFs can melt locally available scrap, reducing reliance on imported coke.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a reverberatory furnace?
options: B) Can handle large volumes of charge
C) No need for refractory lining
quiz.explanation: Reverberatory furnaces have a large hearth and can process large charges.

quiz.q: In a reverberatory furnace, how is heat transferred to the charge?
options: B) Radiation from the roof and walls
quiz.explanation: The roof reflects heat onto the charge, hence 'reverberatory'.

quiz.q: What is a common refractory for the roof of a reverberatory furnace?
quiz.explanation: High-alumina bricks withstand higher temperatures and are used in roofs.

quiz.q: What is the typical fuel consumption of a small reverberatory furnace?
options: A) 0.1â0.5 kg coal per kg metal
B) 1â2 kg coal per kg metal
C) 3â5 kg coal per kg metal
D) 5â10 kg coal per kg metal
quiz.explanation: Reverberatory furnaces are not very efficient, using 1â2 kg coal per kg metal.

quiz.q: Where is a large reverberatory furnace used in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Nkana Smelter in Zambia uses reverberatory furnaces for copper.

quiz.q: What is the main product of flash smelting?
quiz.explanation: Flash smelting produces a matte (metal sulfide) and slag.

quiz.q: What is injected into a flash smelting furnace along with dry concentrate?
quiz.explanation: Oxygen-enriched air or pure oxygen is used to burn the sulfide concentrate.

quiz.q: Why is flash smelting not practical for small-scale operations?
options: A) It requires fine, dry concentrate and gas handling
B) It uses too much electricity
D) It produces too much slag
quiz.explanation: Flash smelting needs sophisticated feed preparation and off-gas treatment.

quiz.q: Where is flash smelting used in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Kansanshi smelter in Zambia uses flash smelting for copper.

quiz.q: What is the main hazard of flash smelting?
quiz.explanation: The off-gas is rich in sulfur dioxide, which is toxic.

quiz.q: What is a crucible furnace best suited for?
options: A) Melting large volumes of iron
B) Melting small amounts of non-ferrous metals
quiz.explanation: Crucible furnaces are ideal for small batches of aluminum, brass, etc.

quiz.q: What material is a crucible typically made of?
quiz.explanation: Crucibles are made of clay-graphite or silicon carbide to withstand high temperatures.

quiz.q: In a cupola furnace, what is the purpose of coke?
options: A) To provide carbon and heat
quiz.explanation: Coke burns to provide heat and also adds carbon to the iron.

quiz.q: What is the typical coke-to-iron ratio in a cupola?
quiz.explanation: A typical cupola uses 1 part coke to 8â12 parts iron.

quiz.q: Why must you never tap molten iron into a wet ladle?
options: A) It will cool too fast
C) It will contaminate the iron
D) It will damage the ladle
quiz.explanation: Water turns to steam explosively when contacted by molten metal.

quiz.q: What is the maximum temperature for fireclay bricks?
quiz.explanation: Fireclay bricks are rated up to about 1200Â°C.

quiz.q: Which refractory is basic and used in steel furnaces?
quiz.explanation: Magnesite bricks are basic and resist basic slags in steelmaking.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an insulating layer in a furnace lining?
quiz.explanation: Insulating layer reduces heat loss through the furnace shell.

quiz.q: Why are expansion joints needed in refractory linings?
options: A) To allow for thermal expansion
quiz.explanation: Bricks expand when heated, so joints prevent cracking.

quiz.q: What safety equipment is needed when cutting refractories?
quiz.explanation: Refractory dust contains silica, so a dust mask is essential.

quiz.q: How long does a furnace lining typically last?
quiz.explanation: Depending on operation, linings last 6â24 months before needing repair.
